results.title: Should Bayesian inference be avoided with a small sample size and weakly informative priors? - Cross Validated
results.content: # Should Bayesian inference be avoided with a small sample size and weakly informative priors? When specifying a Bayesian model, one can specify weakly-informative priors. Given this, if you know beforehand that your priors are weak *and* that you have a small sample size, should you avoid Bayesian inference? $\begingroup$ To the contrary, objective Bayesian priors have the effect of smoothing parameter estimates in small samples and can be helpful. The prior dominates when faced with weak data precisely because there's not much information in the data, so you should depend more on previous knowledge/expectation. Using a prior only when you have strong data is doing Bayesian inference when it is least useful. $\begingroup$ Instead of informative priors, weakly or otherwise, you can also pick non-informative priors. On the other hand, if we don't have a prior that we *trust*, and we're just plugging a prior into our calculations for *convenience*, that's when your concern is valid: When n is small, the posterior can be very sensitive to tiny changes in the prior (even a weakly-informative prior). With small n and no reliable prior, instead of a Bayesian analysis---or even a Frequentist analysis (which may just confirm that "The sample is too small to estimate these parameters with adequate precision")---I would just report descriptive statistics / graphs and be very transparent about the study's limitations: due to the sample size, our results cannot safely generalize to the population, etc. But if we can write down *several* extremely weak priors and we have too little knowledge to confidently choose one of them -- and our sample's so small that the posterior will be sensitive to our choice among these weak priors -- then probably we should indeed do descriptive work or theory instead of inference. Weakly informative priors affect the results weakly. If you used less weakly informative priors, they would affect the result even more. bayesian logistic regression with weakly informative priors (pymc3). 2") How to choose a non-informative or weakly informative hyper priors for my hierarchical bayesian model? 2") Bayesian design for a small sample and how to include informed priors.

results.title: Bayesian Priors in Market Mix Models: Risks, Rewards and Red Flags - Mutinex
results.content: # Bayesian Priors in Market Mix Models: Risks, Rewards and Red Flags. Bayesian priors are a standard component of modern Market Mix Models (MMM), used to improve model stability and incorporate business knowledge. * **Sparse Data:** For a new channel with a limited data history, a prior provides a reasonable starting value for its performance, preventing the model from making unstable estimates. Priors help the model differentiate between the effects of these correlated channels. Priors help the model identify the marketing signal within this noise. **The Prior:** An initial belief about a parameter’s value before analyzing the data. #### **How Strong Priors Degrade Model Quality**. If strong priors are used to lock in the performance of major channels (e.g., Search, TV), they effectively pre-allocate a large portion of the sales results. A well-constructed MMM uses priors as justified and transparent guides; while a model driven by opaque or overly strong priors is not data-driven and presents a significant risk to your business.

results.title: logic - Can evidence with Bayesian reasoning change your priors? - Philosophy Stack Exchange
results.content: # Can evidence with Bayesian reasoning change your priors? My question is not about whether your prior beliefs should change to new beliefs under Bayesian reasoning, which is an obvious "yes." Rather, what I mean is: is there room in Bayesian reasoning for a situation where you start with one prior belief, and then some evidence comes in which makes you realize, not that you should adjust your belief in one way or another from your prior prior belief based on that evidence, but that your initial belief should simply be abandoned in favor of some alternative? You now don't use Bayesian calculation to update your prior of 50%, but abandon that in favor of a new 17% prior for green. Now, possibly what they are thinking is that Case 2 does involve a calculated Bayesian update, it's just that the calculation is a trivial one: if the probability that I would perceive 17 green balls when there aren't 17 balls it sufficiently low, it moves any prior belief in the probability of drawing green (between 0 and 1) to very close to 17%. Perhaps part of my puzzlement is over the idea that the numbers for a Bayesian calculation in case 1 are very well-defined, so we know exactly how to apply the update formula, but if we try that for case 2, it is far from clear how to assign a probability for my perceptions (or testimony from others, or whatever else I based my priors on) being accurate. In such cases subjective Bayesians must create a new prior. Bayesian approach can be seen as updating *prior* beliefs. This is the equivalent of the behavior of a political, religious, or philosophic ideologue, who in this case is a devotee of Redism, and has a Bayesian prior that all balls are red, and any counter-evidence is downweighed by the (almost certainty inappropriate, but priors ARE judgement calls!) extremely high confidence in the prior. I know of no case where you can have loops (which are the updaters of the original "priors") If you did you would start having to worry about the new Bayesian "Graph" will settle on a "solution".

results.title: 7 Key Insights on Noninformative Priors in Bayesian Methods
results.content: # 7 Key Insights on Noninformative Priors in Bayesian Methods. > **Discover essential insights behind noninformative priors in Bayesian analysis.**. With noninformative priors, even with limited data, the conclusion strives to remain as unbiased as possible, thus reflecting more accurately the information content in the data itself. The use of noninformative priors in Bayesian analysis offers several clear advantages:. When comparing models, noninformative priors help ensure that differences in the conclusions are primarily due to the data and not because of strong prior assumptions. In survival analysis, crucial parameters like the baseline hazard rate might be modeled with noninformative priors to avoid assumptions about the underlying distribution. By employing noninformative priors, researchers can pursue more data-driven conclusions without the sway of possibly unsound or overly specific assumptions inherent in informative priors. By carefully considering the definition, core assumptions, inherent advantages, and practical limitations of noninformative priors, researchers can design Bayesian models that aspire to objective, data-driven inference.

results.title: Bayesian Dynamic Borrowing with Robust Mixture Priors: Fair or not? - general - Datamethods Discussion Forum
results.content: This is a place where statisticians, epidemiologists, informaticists, machine learning practitioners, and other research methodologists communicate with themselves and with clinical, translational, and health services researchers to discuss issues related to data: research methods, quantitative methods, study design, measurement, statistical analysis, interpretation of data and statistical results, clinical trials, journal articles, statistical graphics, causal inference, medical decision making, and more. # Bayesian Dynamic Borrowing with Robust Mixture Priors: Fair or not? I am a statistician on the sponsor side of trials, having recently graduated from school and working a good bit in Bayesian methods, and Bayesian Dynamic Borrowing has become a popular topic in my current work. For example, a “robust mixture prior” uses a mixture prior, one vague piece and one informative piece, each with weight adding to 1, and if your data coming in “agrees” with the informative piece of the prior, you update the weights on your prior to favor the informative piece. If the data does not agree with the informative piece of the prior, then the vague piece is given higher weight. A few of Frank Harrell’s resources and posts on Bayesian methods have mentioned that one way to cheat as a Bayesian is to change the prior after seeing the data. Once to weight the prior, and once as the data itself (likelihood). The defense is that there are no further “user choices” being made, the method is only specified one time at the beginning, and the weights are updated “automatically” as data comes in. It still seems like the prior is technically being updated and data is being counted twice. I was wondering if anyone had any more thoughts on this topic, especially any specific examples that say Dynamic Borrowing is fair or not. A prior distribution is specified before the data. If you are computing a posterior from the initial prior (not re-weighted) that strikes me as coherent and fair. If you are computing a posterior from the re-weighted prior, that strikes me as cheating. You might find this paper by Arnold Zellner, who discussed Bayesian methods from the info processing perspective interesting.
